Receive Channel Messages as a Promise or a Stream

Source: R/promise.R
mizu_recv_async.Rd

mizu_recv_async() returns a promises::promise() immediately, without blocking. The promise resolves with the next received payload, the same R object a blocking mizu_recv() would have returned, zero-copy ALTREP views included. Chain it with promises::then() or the promise pipe %...>%.

Usage

mizu_recv_async(ch, timeout = Inf)

mizu_recv_handler(ch, fn, batch = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'mizu_channel'
as.promise(x)

# S3 method for class 'mizu_channel'
is.promising(x)

Arguments

ch

a channel handle from mizu_channel() (or the ch binding inside a peer expression). Arming a spin channel errors: its publish path skips the wake checkpoint by design.

timeout

seconds after which the promise rejects with the mizu_timeout classed error. Inf (the default) waits indefinitely.

fn

a function(x) called with each received message (or, with batch = TRUE, each burst as one list), and finally with a terminal condition. NULL removes the handler.

batch

deliver each drained burst to fn as one list in a single call, instead of one call per message.

x

for the as.promise method: a channel handle, treated as mizu_recv_async(x).

Value

mizu_recv_async(): a promises::promise() resolving with the next message. mizu_recv_handler(): the channel handle, invisibly.

Details

The promise rejects on mizu_closed, mizu_peer_gone, and timeout expiry with classed error conditions that carry the same class names as the sentinels, so inherits(x, "mizu_closed") works on either form. Close and peer death wake the event loop directly, so the rejection is prompt rather than waiting for the timeout.

Several outstanding calls on one channel resolve in FIFO call order, one message each. No message is lost: messages already in the ring resolve immediately (still asynchronously, as promises require), and only messages yet to arrive wait on the event.

mizu_recv_handler() is the stream form. It installs fn on the channel, and the event loop delivers each burst of messages to it without allocating a promise per message. With batch = TRUE, each drained burst is delivered as one list in a single fn(list) call, which is the high-throughput form. With batch = FALSE, fn(value) is called once per message. Close and peer death are delivered to fn as the classed error conditions (mizu_closed, mizu_peer_gone), after which the handler is removed. A declined foreign payload (see mizu_send()) is delivered as its mizu_error_python_payload condition and the handler continues. An error raised by fn removes the handler and propagates at the event loop. mizu_recv_handler(ch, NULL) removes the handler.

A channel message belongs to whoever takes it first. A channel can have only one of the two consumer forms at a time: installing a handler while promises are pending, or requesting a promise while a handler is installed, is an error. A blocking mizu_recv() mixed with either consumer form consumes in arrival order, so the blocking call may take a message that a promise or the handler was waiting on. A close or peer death that it observes is observed by the consumer too, because both are channel state, re-read on every receive and never consumed. (A task result instead belongs to exactly one consumer; see mizu_collect_all_async().)

Every main-thread drain is bounded per event-loop turn and re-scheduled, so a saturated ring starves neither Shiny nor later::run_now().

Requires the later package, and promises for mizu_recv_async().

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive() && requireNamespace("promises", quietly = TRUE)
library(promises)
ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_recv_async(ch) %...>% print()
mizu_send(ch, 42L)
later::run_now()
mizu_close(ch)
}
